title: CheckoutSwitch: How fake delivery fees disguise online purchases
summary: Gen Threat Labs uncovered how fake delivery notices and prize notifications trick people into paying for products they never intended to buy.
body_markdown:
By[Martin Chlumecký](https://www.gendigital.com/blog/authors/martin-chlumecky)


,[Luis Corrons](https://www.gendigital.com/blog/authors/luis-corrons)


> **What you need to know**
>
>
> **The risk:** CheckoutSwitch campaigns use fake parcel notices, prize offers and cloud-storage warnings to request small payments. Gen Threat Labs traced payment requests to unrelated merchants selling different products or services, from Weber barbecue grills to Oral-B toothbrushes. In one case, personal details entered on fake DHL pages also appeared in a retailer's customer account.
>
>
> **The scale:** Gen observes 1.2 million unique emails from these campaigns daily, reaching 200,000 to 300,000 customers each day within our protected customer base alone.
>
>
> **Our advice:** Verify unexpected delivery notices, offers and account warnings through the company's official website or app before entering personal or card details. Even a small fee can expose you to unwanted charges and misuse of your information.


Our investigation began with a German-language email promising a Weber Spirit grill. The message claimed to be a promotion from Hagebau, a well-known hardware retailer in Germany, and told the recipient they had already won their new grill.


The offer fit the summer barbecue season and borrowed the credibility of two familiar brands. It also contradicted itself: elsewhere in the same message claiming the recipient had won one, the person was urged to hurry for a chance to win.


It was the kind of spam offer we see regularly, and our protections were already blocking this type of activity. Recognizing the deception, however, told us little about the business behind the scam. We wanted to understand how these campaigns turned someone's interest in a free grill into money, and what happened to the information collected along the way.


We began checking how widely the campaign was circulating and following its links. The grill offer connected to infrastructure carrying promotions under other brands, including offers for Oral-B dental kits. As we examined more messages, we found retail prizes, parcel delivery notifications and warnings that cloud accounts or personal files were about to disappear.


Some destinations complicated the picture. An antivirus-expiry warning redirected us to McAfee's official website, raising the possibility that deceptive messages were being used to generate sales for genuine commercial services. Identifying a fake email was only the beginning of understanding that relationship.


We followed selected campaigns through to checkout and examined the payment attempts they generated. The merchant records allowed us to identify the scam businesses requesting the money and compare what they offered with what the emails had promised.


In a campaign using DHL branding, that trail led us to a retailer's customer account containing the details we had entered during a supposed parcel-delivery process.


## A €9.99 delivery fee, and a shop we had never visited


The DHL-themed pages showed a parcel containing an Apple iPad Pro. They took us through delivery questions and asked for our contact details and address, followed by a €9.99 payment to release the shipment.


Figure 1. The fake DHL pages show a parcel containing an iPad Pro and request delivery confirmation. English translation: “Delivery pending”; “Please confirm your delivery details on the next page”; “Package information”; “Shipping costs: outstanding”.


During our research, we recorded the resulting card authorization request. It named PXT*gearteria.com, an online retailer unrelated to DHL. The merchant identifier connected the payment request to that business.


Figure 2. The checkout requests €9.99 and collects contact and delivery details.


**Recorded field** **Value**


Merchant PXT*gearteria.com


Merchant identifier 66172614


Amount requested €9.99


Record type Card authorization request


We wanted to see whether Gearteria had recorded an order. The shop offered the option to create an account automatically at checkout, so we wondered whether one had been created with our details. We hadn't received an account confirmation, but we tried resetting the password using the email address we had entered on the fake DHL pages. The reset worked, and when we signed in, we found the name and street address we had given for the delivery.


Figure 3. The Gearteria customer account contained the name and address we entered during the fake DHL delivery process.


The delivery pages had collected information under DHL's identity. We could now see that information in another retailer's customer records, despite never having knowingly registered there.


Someone receiving this message could be left waiting for a parcel while an unrelated business held their details in a shopping account they knew nothing about.


We are calling this pattern **CheckoutSwitch** . The payment is presented as a delivery fee, prize shipping or another small expense, while the merchant requesting the money is associated with a different product or service.


## Following the commission


The redirects between the emails and their destinations carried affiliate identifiers. These record which partner referred someone to a merchant, allowing that partner to earn a commission when the referral produces a qualifying purchase or subscription.


Affiliate marketing gives businesses a way to pay partners for bringing them customers. In the campaigns we investigated, those customers were being recruited through false offers and warnings. The reason they had been given to pay could have little connection to the product or service associated with the merchant.


The DHL case shows how that works. The delivery pages asked for €9.99 to release a parcel. Gearteria then requested the same amount through its merchant account. Someone following those pages could agree to the payment without ever having chosen to buy anything from Gearteria.


Matching the amount helps preserve the deception. The visitor has already accepted €9.99 as a delivery expense, so the price itself gives them no reason to question the transaction. Across the campaigns we observed, the requested fees ranged from US$3 to US$20. These relatively small amounts may attract less scrutiny and make payment more likely. Affiliate tracking allows the referral to be credited to the partner that brought them there, with a commission earned on a qualifying purchase.


This gives the operators a way to make money from the misleading promotion. A fake prize offer or delivery problem can bring someone into a commercial checkout, even though they have been given a false explanation for the purchase.


Following the affiliate identifiers alongside the payment records allowed us to connect those promotions with the merchants requesting the money.


## An iPad prize, a fitness plan


A campaign impersonating Walmart offered another view of the same process. After a "spin-to-win" promotion, the visitor was told they had won an Apple iPad and needed to pay $9.97 for shipping.


Figure 4. The Walmart-themed prize page claims the visitor has won an Apple iPad Pro.


The payment attempt we recorded named BestFitMen.com. On that merchant's website, we found a one-time fitness plan delivered by email for $9.97, exactly the amount requested to ship the supposed prize.


Figure 5. BestFitMen’s one-time fitness plan, shown on the left, costs $9.97, matching the requested shipping fee.


The Walmart promotion had given the recipient no reason to expect a fitness purchase. Following the payment request revealed a merchant selling an unrelated product at the same price.


An Oral-B reward campaign using UnitedHealthcare branding produced a similar result. It offered a dental kit after a survey and requested $9.95 for shipping. The authorization request named a supplement merchant whose website advertised a product for $9.95.


Across these cases, the requested amount fit the story on the page closely enough to look like a small delivery expense. Examining the merchant revealed what else that money could be buying.


## Paying to save your files


Cloud-storage campaigns used warnings about full accounts, failed backups and imminent file deletion to bring people to a payment page. Some displayed countdowns or claimed that automated deletion was already underway.


Figure 6. A cloud-storage warning threatens automatic file deletion and displays a countdown.


In one route we investigated, a €6.99 authorization request named CARVEPLAZA.COM, a website presented as an arts-and-crafts retailer. Another led to TopTV.site, an unrelated shopping membership service.


Other redirects took us to NordLocker, a genuine cloud-storage provider. Purchasing storage there would not resolve the alleged problem with the account described in the original warning.


We had already followed an antivirus-expiry warning to McAfee's official website. Alongside the unrelated shops, we were finding genuine services being promoted through misleading emails.


Anyone can include a link to a company's official website in an email. The messages below used familiar technology brands but came from unrelated domains. If a message says your subscription is expiring or your account needs attention, check the sender's full email address, then open the company's website or app yourself to check your account.


Figure 7. Email using the names and branding of technology companies, sent from unrelated domains.


## The activity behind the emails


Within Gen's protected customer base, we observe **1.2 million unique emails from these campaigns each day, reaching 200,000 to 300,000 customers daily** .


These figures cover only the emails we observe among Gen's protected customers. The actual worldwide volume is much higher.


The messages borrowed identities across several industries. Delivery lures used DHL, UPS, DPD and La Poste. Retail promotions and reward offers used names including Hagebau, Lidl, Walmart, Weber and Oral-B. Other messages impersonated healthcare services or used antivirus, streaming and cloud-account warnings. Whatever the brand, the narratives played on a few basic emotions: fear of losing something, such as personal files or a held parcel, and hope of gaining something, such as a prize or payout. These emotions drove both the click and the payment.


For a separate analysis, we randomly selected about 33,000 emails per day over one month. The resulting dataset contained **1,090,839 unique emails** . Our classification showed that the traffic was overwhelmingly abusive: **59% was deceptive affiliate marketing, 25% was likely scams and 16% was suspicious affiliate marketing** . Most of the emails we analyzed fell into two categories: deceptive affiliate marketing and likely scams.


In a separate analysis of the same dataset, we found that **98% of emails contained at least one Google Cloud Storage link** . These links redirected visitors through tracking and affiliate systems to an offer or checkout. Serving as the entry point to the affiliate network, they may help campaigns bypass spam and other email filters. Gen Security solutions already block this activity, even when the initial link uses a trusted cloud domain.


The language distribution was heavily concentrated in English (51%) and French (35%), which together accounted for most of the analyzed emails. Italian, German, Spanish and Dutch followed at much lower levels. The narratives also varied by language: fake-prize offers dominated several European languages, particularly French and Italian, while English-language emails showed a broader mix of fake prizes and cloud-storage warnings.


Threat prevalence shows a clear geographic concentration in Western and English-speaking markets. The highest prevalence was observed in the United Kingdom, followed by Australia and the Netherlands, with the United States, France, Austria, Belgium, Canada and Switzerland also ranking prominently. Italy, Spain, Portugal and Germany showed more moderate prevalence, while substantially lower levels were observed across most measured markets in Asia, Latin America and Eastern Europe.


Figure 8. Global distribution of threat prevalence across protected users.


Over the last four months, threat prevalence remained broadly stable, with only moderate fluctuations and no pronounced peaks. The pattern does not indicate strong event-driven or seasonal surges, suggesting that the threat is persistent and significant, rather than concentrating around major holidays or marketing events.


## How the campaigns use familiar brands


Looking at the original email alone would not reveal the merchant eventually requesting payment. Following those routes allowed us to connect familiar-looking promotions with the commercial destinations behind them.


Some brands provide the identity behind the message. A fake DHL notification presents a delivery problem, while a Netflix renewal warning claims that an account needs attention. The recipient is given a reason to act through a service they recognize.


Other brands make the offer attractive. The grill email that started our investigation used Hagebau as the retailer behind the promotion and Weber as the promised prize. Similar campaigns offered Oral-B dental kits, Makita tools and Apple iPads.


News organizations appear in another role. Fake articles using CNN or CBS News branding present health-product promotions as reporting, borrowing the credibility of a familiar news source.


A single campaign can therefore involve several brands with different purposes. In the Walmart example, the promotion used Walmart's identity and offered an Apple iPad, while the payment request came from BestFitMen.


The following names appear in the documented campaign examples:


**Category** **Brands and services** **How they appear**


Retailers Hagebau, Lidl, Leroy Merlin, Walmart, Amazon, Costco, Lowe's, Ace Hardware, Tractor Supply, Decathlon, Jumbo, Sephora Fake promotions, surveys, rewards and prize notifications


Products offered as bait Weber, Oral-B, Silvercrest, Makita, Dexter, Kobalt, Quechua, BLACK+DECKER, YETI, Philips, Lancôme, Apple's iPad, LG, Dell, Nike Products advertised as prizes, gifts or items awaiting delivery


Delivery services DHL, FedEx, UPS, DPD, La Poste Fake parcel notifications, delivery confirmation and fee requests


Healthcare UnitedHealthcare, Doctolib, MioDottore, MyChart, Pharmacie Lafayette, 1177 Medical-kit rewards, surveys and healthcare-themed offers


Motoring and roadside services VINCI Autoroutes, Telepass, CAA, ANWB, ADAC Branded rewards, surveys and equipment offers


Security software Norton, Avast, McAfee Subscription-expiry warnings, failed-payment notices and renewal offers


Streaming services Netflix, Canal+, Paramount+, King IPTV, SiriusXM, Trex IPTV Account-renewal warnings and loyalty rewards


Cloud storage and account services Apple/iCloud, Google/Gmail, generic "Cloud Storage" identities Storage-full warnings, threatened file deletion and account-support messages


News organizations CNN, CBS News Fake articles and medical-authority claims promoting supplements


Gambling Raging Bull Casino, BettyWins, Need4Spins, Limitless, Slots of Vegas, Lussurio Claims that a payout is waiting, leading to registration and deposit offers


## What people and businesses stand to lose


The risks extend beyond the initial shipping fee. People can lose money on purchases they never intended to make, and some destinations introduce membership or recurring-payment terms. Providing card details through a deceptive process also exposes that information to possible theft or misuse.


The Gearteria account showed a further consequence we could document directly: personal information collected during a fake delivery process appearing in an unrelated customer profile. That reuse creates risks of impersonation and identity fraud. A profile created without someone's knowledge also raises the risk that terms and conditions they have never seen could be accepted on their behalf, including automatic renewal of services and recurring charges. The profile itself was an observed finding. Acceptance of such terms, automatic renewal and subsequent identity theft were not established by our research.


The companies being impersonated can suffer reputational damage and receive complaints about offers or charges they had nothing to do with.


Merchants receiving the referrals may also face consequences. A business that has not approved these methods could pay affiliate commissions for customers who were deceived about the purchase, then have to handle complaints, refunds and chargebacks.


Consumers can check the original claim before entering their details. A delivery notification can be verified through the courier's official website or app. A storage warning can be checked by opening the account independently. Unexpected promotions can be verified through the named company's own channels.


## The business behind the spam


What began with a grill offer led us to campaigns connecting familiar brands with unrelated commercial transactions. The payment records identified the merchants requesting the money, while affiliate tracking showed how referrals were credited. In the DHL case, we could also see where the personal information had gone.


Someone agreeing to a small delivery fee can end up buying an unrelated product or service. A merchant paying affiliates in good faith may also be misled, funding promotions that deceive the customers it is paying to attract.


Businesses need to examine the emails and pages generating those referrals and check what customers were promised before they arrived. In the campaigns we followed, someone arriving as a customer could still believe they were simply paying to receive a parcel.
